faq.q: What is the green coating on copper?
faq.a: It is a patina, also called verdigris, made mostly of copper carbonate and copper sulfate minerals formed by air and rain reacting with the copper.

faq.q: How long does copper take to turn green?
faq.a: It goes brown and dark within months, but a full green patina usually takes years to decades, depending on the weather and air.
asks: How quickly does copper go green?

faq.q: Does the green layer harm the copper?
faq.a: No, it protects it. Unlike rust on iron, the patina sticks tightly and shields the copper underneath from further corrosion.
asks: Is the green on copper bad?

faq.q: Why is the Statue of Liberty green?
faq.a: Its skin is thin copper. When it was unveiled in 1886 it was shiny brown, and over about 30 years it weathered to the green patina we see today.
asks: Was the Statue of Liberty always green?

faq.q: Why do copper coins turn brown?
faq.a: Oxygen in the air forms a thin layer of copper oxide on the surface, which looks dull brown. Over longer times outdoors they can go green too.

facts: The Statue of Liberty's copper skin was shiny brown in 1886 and had turned green within about 30 years.
The Statue of Liberty's copper skin is only about 2.4 millimetres thick.

quiz.say: Why don't people scrub the green patina off copper roofs?
quiz.show: Why don't people scrub the green patina off copper roofs?
quiz.why: The tight patina layer shields the copper from further corrosion, so the roof lasts longer.

wrong.0: The patina is left on because it is protective, not because it cannot be touched.
wrong.1: The green is formed by the copper reacting with air and rain, not painted on.
